demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
**Patient Vignette: Aisha, Age 33**

Aisha sits forward in the chair, her hands clasped tightly in her lap, the muscles in her jaw working even when she isn't speaking. She is a park ranger, a job she has held for eight years, and she describes it with a quiet, matter-of-fact pride. She knows the trails of the national forest like the lines on her own palms, can identify a bird by its call, and has always found a deep, steadying peace in the silence of the woods. That peace is gone now.

The trauma happened fourteen months ago. Aisha’s younger brother, Kofi, was an assistant guide on her team. He was twenty-seven, exuberant, and had the kind of laugh that made you feel like everything was going to be okay. They were leading a dawn hike for a group of schoolchildren. The trail was wet from a night of rain. Kofi was at the back of the line, helping a boy whose boot had come untied. Aisha was fifty yards ahead, pointing out a red-tailed hawk.

She heard the sound first. A low, grinding groan of rock, then a wet, heavy thud. She turned to see a section of the hillside, loosened by the rain, had given way. A cascade of mud and stone poured down, not a massive landslide, but enough. Enough to catch Kofi and the boy. Aisha remembers screaming his name. She remembers digging with her bare hands, the mud cold and sucking at her fingers, while one of the teachers called for help. She found the boy first—scared, muddy, but alive. She found Kofi three minutes later. He was pinned by a boulder the size of a cooler. His head was at an unnatural angle. She knew immediately. She held his hand until the paramedics arrived, but he was gone. The official cause was a traumatic brain injury. For Aisha, the cause is that she was looking at a bird while her brother died.

Now, Aisha cannot be still. In our sessions, she describes a relentless, buzzing current of guilt that runs beneath everything. She replays the morning in a loop. She calculates the steps she could have taken. *If I had walked slower. If I had made him take the lead. If I had watched the weather report more closely.* She doesn't just think these thoughts; she feels them in her body. Her chest tightens, her palms sweat, and she feels a cold wash of nausea every time she hears a sudden noise—a car backfiring, a dropped book, a child’s shout in the grocery store.

Her work has become a minefield. She requested a desk assignment, but the park is understaffed, and she feels a crushing obligation to her team. The first time she went back on the trail, she saw the scar on the hillside and froze. Her heart hammered so hard she thought she might faint. Now, she forces herself to go, but she is hypervigilant. She scans every slope, every overhang. She cannot hear the sound of gravel crunching under a boot without flinching. She avoids the section of trail where it happened, taking a two-mile detour that adds an hour to her patrol. Her supervisor has noticed. She told him she was training for a marathon.

At home, her husband, David, tries to reach her, but she feels like she is living behind a pane of glass. He touches her arm, and she feels nothing. He asks how her day was, and she says, “Fine,” because the truth—that she spent eight hours waiting for the ground to swallow her—is too heavy to speak. She has stopped sleeping in their bed. She sleeps on the couch, with the television on low, because the silence of their bedroom is too much like the silence on the trail after the noise stopped. The only time she feels any relief is when she is running, running so hard that her lungs burn and her legs ache, running until the only thing she can hear is her own ragged breath, drowning out the sound of the rocks falling.
